items.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial
items.summary:
On treacherous political terrain, the government is right to want to proceed with caution and at a pace of its own choosing

During the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union.

Mindful of the unique capacity of the Brexit debate to divide and polarise, Andy Burnham appears, for the time being, to be adopting a version of this strategy. On Friday, the prime minister rightly hailed the signing of a reset deal with the EU on food exports, emissions trading and youth mobility as a “good day” for the UK. He then reiterated that further discussion was needed on finding the right long-term relationship with Brussels.

Continue reading...

The blocked provisions of the law, passed in May, set statewide use-of-force standards, gave state officials authority to investigate and prosecute certain cases involving federal officers — such as excessive use-of-force incidents — and restricted federal officers’ use of face coverings. Oliver wrote that the sections likely violate the Constitution’s supremacy clause, which limits states’ ability to control federal operations.

items.title: Kemi is beside herself that Burnham is trying to salvage a Brexit deal. Can’t we all stop talking about it? | John Crace
items.summary:
Badenoch ends her anti-EU speech by calling herself ‘the leader of common sense’. Really?

When you’ve got David Cameron, Theresa May, Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak saying you’ve got it wrong on Brexit, then the chances are Andy Burnham must be doing something right. These four are the former prime ministers that are largely responsible for the mess the UK is currently in. Lord Big Dave had never really given the possibility of leaving the EU much thought. The Maybot spent three years saying nothing more intelligent than “Brexit means Brexit”. Boris lied through his teeth to get his deal over the line. And as for Rishi? It’s hard to think of anything he achieved.

All of which makes life tricky for Kemi Badenoch. Because in an ideal world, Kemi would rather we all forgot about Brexit entirely. Not because it is going so well, but because it it isn’t. She would like you to believe that Brexit was nothing to do with her – even though she was a hardline Brexiter – or the Tories. Rather it was some kind of paranormal event that just happened to the country while the Conservatives were in power. Correlation does not imply causality and all that. In KemiWorld we would pretend that everything is more or less OK and that the noblest course of action is to live with the self-inflicted injury.

items.title: The Guardian view on Ofsted: its damaged relationship with schools in England needs fixing | Editorial
items.summary:
The government, as well as the inspectorate, must take responsibility for reforms that have not worked out

The inspection and rating of schools is, by definition, a fraught process. There are few things that parents care more about than the education of their children. For teachers and headteachers, it is stressful and exposing to have their work judged. At a time when shrinking school rolls are leading to closures, the stakes are even higher. An unpopular school with empty places is far more likely to be asked to merge, or close, than one that is sought after by parents.

Policymakers have a tough job to strike a balance between the undeniable pressure that the watchdog places on schools in England and the benefits to families of information to aid their choices. But the coroner’s verdict on the death of Ruth Perry, a headteacher who took her own life in 2023, tipped the balance away from a system that relied too heavily on one-word judgments. Word spread quickly, and now Sharratt sees many members of the community, which numbers in the hundreds.

items.title: Newsom's bid to empty California's death row collides with voters' repeated rejection of abolition
items.summary:
A lawsuit challenging Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom's plan to commute 548 death sentences is raising questions about the governor's clemency powers, with a legal expert arguing Newsom is using his gubernatorial authority to circumvent the will of voters who have repeatedly rejected efforts to abolish capital punishment.

Newsom announced Nov. 5 that he intends to commute the death sentences of all 548 inmates on the Golden State's death row to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole, a move that will take effect only after the necessary legal steps are completed.

The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation (CJLF) on Sunday filed a lawsuit at the California Supreme Court seeking to block Newsom's proposed sweeping commutation, citing the governor's "failure to provide legally required notice to district attorneys and his disregard for the rights of victims and their families to be notified and heard," according to a news release.

Newsom may be using clemency to impose his own views on capital punishment despite voters repeatedly rejecting abolition, Zack Smith, a senior legal fellow for Courts and the Constitution at the Heritage Foundation, told Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

Yet investors in a failed Obama-era solar plant are questioning why President Donald Trump's own Justice Department is fighting to squash their fraud lawsuit over a $275 million federal grant — a case they say could recover up to $1 billion for taxpayers.

The investors allege that Spanish construction giant ACS and companies to tied its former subsidiary Cobra, misled federal officials into approving the grant by claiming the troubled solar plant was ready for use, even though it had suffered major construction problems and was shut down for months following a molten-salt-tank failure.

The lawsuit centers on the beleaguered Crescent Dunes solar plant, a billion-dollar, government-backed project that began operating in Nevada in 2015 but was later plagued by engineering failures, repeated shutdowns and two bankruptcies before being sold for just $7 million in July.

items.title: If Democrats want to win, blue-collar populists are the key | Dustin Guastella and Jared Abbott
items.summary:
Our analysis shows that ‘Bernie-Dog’ candidates are the most underrated success stories in US politics

Democrats had a huge night on 3 November. The party ran an average of about 15 points ahead of Kamala Harris’s 2024 margins, and picked up seats that Trump carried by double digits just two years ago.

Of course, the size and scope of the blue wave make it hard to draw specific lessons, and the results will inevitably serve as a Rorschach test reflecting each commentator’s prior beliefs. Democrats of all stripes won elections in all sorts of unlikely places.

items.title: Trump inspired a blue revolution. Can Democrats meet the moment? | Dana R Fisher
items.summary:
Political participation – in meetings, boycotts and demonstrations – has increased since Trump took office. It’s time for change

Over the past two years, Americans have watched as the Trump administration enacted Project 2025 and the US has descended into a state of lawless authoritarianism. Instead of sinking into a state of paralysis, though, Americans rose up to push back against the attacks, including limitations of voting rights and manipulations of political power through the gerrymandering of congressional districts.

Donald Trump’s actions motivated resistance in the streets in the form of large-scale public demonstrations, along with more localized mobilizations against ICE and the occupation of American cities. On 3 November, the collective response manifested as resistance at the ballot box.

items.title: After a blue wave, Trump will dig in his heels. We must be more vigilant than ever | Steve Cohen and Michael Shank
items.summary:
Anti-democratic behaviors won’t disappear overnight. The new Congress – and all of us – must rise to the occasion

Americans just witnessed a blue tsunami in the midterm elections, with historic firsts across many US states: the country’s first female Black governor, first female Native American governor, first Muslim US senator, and more.

And while the voters’ repudiation of Donald Trump’s agenda is clear, as Democrats seize the majority of both chambers of Congress, the work to defend our institutions from further democratic backsliding won’t ease up overnight.
